fields.Front: What are the building blocks of the hierarchical model?
fields.Back: RECORDS, grouped into record types (all department records form the DEPARTMENT record type), and PARENT-CHILD RELATIONSHIPS (PCRs). A PCR type is a 1:M relationship between two record types, one parent and one child ('a department has many employees'). An OCCURRENCE of a PCR type is one parent record together with a number of records of the child type. The whole database forms a TREE.

fields.Front: What three situations does the hierarchical model have trouble modelling, and why?
fields.Back:
1. M:N relationships (Employee WORKS ON Project) - a tree edge is always 1:M
2. A record type that is a child in more than one PCR type - a record can have only one parent in a tree, but EMPLOYEE is naturally a child of DEPARTMENT and of PROJECT
3. N-ary relationships with more than two participating record types

fields.Front: In the hierarchical company tree, where is the same employee's data stored three times, and what is the instructor's rule of thumb?
fields.Back: As an employee under the DEPARTMENT; again as a SUPERVISEE under another employee (SSN and name stored twice); and again as a WORKER under each project worked on. A name change must be made in every copy. Her rule: 'in a really good model for a database you don't have to store things twice.'

fields.Front: How does the hierarchical model map an M:N relationship, and how does the instructor summarise the model?
fields.Back: Only 1:N can be modelled, so the M:N relationship is represented AS IF it were 1:N, using POINTERS (virtual/logical child records in IMS) to point back at the real record instead of duplicating it. Her summary: it 'was great with one-to-many relationships, but for many-to-many it had to make up this weird pointer to make things work' - and it pushes the navigation onto the programmer.

fields.Front: What are the building blocks of the network model, and what are the three elements of a set type?
fields.Back:
RECORDS (classified into record types, like a struct) and SETS. A SET TYPE is a 1:N relationship between two record types with three elements:
1. A NAME for the set
2. An OWNER record type (the 'one' side)
3. A MEMBER record type (the 'many' side)

fields.Front: List the navigation operations the network model supports, and what is wrong with them?
fields.Back: Given an owner, find all members of the set occurrence; given an owner, find the first / nth / last member; given a member, find the next or previous member; given a member, find the owner. Every one is a NAVIGATION operation - the programmer walks pointer to pointer, and a new question means a new program. Her example set occurrence: a course (owner) with the students registered in it (members).

fields.Front: What three problems did Codd's relational model solve, and how does it represent a database?
fields.Back: It got rid of the issue with many-to-many relationships; it 'glued everything together nicely' so queries were still possible; and it avoided redundancy. The database is a COLLECTION OF RELATIONS: each relation is a table, a set of rows, each row a collection of related data values. No pointers, trees or linked lists are visible - only tables, rows, columns and cells.

fields.Front: What analogy does the instructor use for the relational model, and when does it fall short?
fields.Back: It is 'the Meryl Streep of acting or the Beatles of rock and roll' of databases - one of the things from computer science that will stay with you for your whole career. It falls short at massive (Google-scale) data volumes, which is why NoSQL databases were developed; 'most reasonably sized companies will still use a relational database as their main primary database.'

fields.Front: APPLICATION: match the model to its date, inventor and DBMS - hierarchical, network, relational, ER.
fields.Back:
Hierarchical: IBM IMS (no single date given; the older model).
Network: CODASYL committee, 1971, DBMS IDMS.
Relational: Codd, 1970, most DBMSs today.
ER model: Peter Chen, 1976 (Week 1).
Mixing up these dates and names is a stated exam trap.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §1.7.1, §2.6): what does the textbook add about the hierarchical and network models, and where does it cover them?
fields.Back:
It calls both LEGACY DATA MODELS and classifies them as REPRESENTATIONAL (implementation) or RECORD-BASED data models - the same category as the relational model, which is why all three are directly implementable while the ER model is not.
The network model's full name is the CODASYL DBTG model (Conference on Data Systems Languages, Database Task Group); its DML was proposed in the 1971 DBTG Report as an extension of COBOL and is RECORD-AT-A-TIME, which is the formal name for the instructor's 'navigation'.
The hierarchical model has NO STANDARD LANGUAGE; IMS's DL/1 was the de facto industry standard, and IMS dominated the DBMS market for over twenty years, 1965-1985.
A third early family also existed: INVERTED FILE systems.
Coverage in the assigned reading is only §1.7.1 and §2.6; full chapters live in the book's online appendices D and E, so Lesson 1 is examined from the slides.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §1.7.1): beyond redundancy and trouble with M:N relationships, why were the early models replaced?
fields.Back:
Because they INTERMIXED CONCEPTUAL RELATIONSHIPS WITH THE PHYSICAL STORAGE AND PLACEMENT OF RECORDS ON DISK - a student's grade records might literally be stored next to the student record. That gave excellent performance for the queries the database was designed for, but poor DATA ABSTRACTION and PROGRAM-DATA INDEPENDENCE: new queries needing a different physical organization were hard to run efficiently, and reorganizing when requirements changed was laborious.
They also offered ONLY PROGRAMMING-LANGUAGE INTERFACES, so every new query meant writing, testing and debugging a new program.
The relational model was proposed to separate physical storage from the conceptual representation, to give data representation a mathematical foundation, and to introduce HIGH-LEVEL QUERY LANGUAGES so that a new question no longer meant a new program.

fields.Text: The two data models used before the relational model were the {{c1::hierarchical}} model (most popular DBMS: IBM's {{c1::IMS}}, still used in banks and airlines) and the {{c1::network}} model (designed by the CODASYL committee in 1971; a popular DBMS is IDMS).

Unlike the hierarchical model, a network record type can be owner or member in {{c1::any number}} of set types, so a record can have several 'parents' (no {{c1::tree}} restriction); each set occurrence is physically a {{c1::circular linked list}} from the owner through the members and back.

The instructor says you do {{c1::not}} need to know how to map an ER diagram to the {{c1::network}} model; what you must know is the two older models, their {{c1::building blocks}} and why they struggled (with many-to-many relationships and repeated data).

The relational model was introduced by {{c1::E. F. (Ted) Codd}} in {{c1::1970}}, a {{c1::mathematician}} and former professor working at IBM; his famous paper was 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'. Most DBMSs today are based on it.

Textbook (Chapter 5 opening): the relational model's theoretical basis is {{c1::set theory and first-order predicate logic}}; the first commercial implementations arrived in the {{c1::early 1980s}} (IBM's SQL/DS on MVS, and Oracle); and Codd was later given the {{c1::Turing Award}} for the work.

Textbook (Elmasri §1.7.6, §2.6): the book spells it {{c1::NOSQL}} and reads the acronym as {{c1::'Not Only SQL'}} - some of an organization's data sits in SQL systems and some in NOSQL systems, depending on the application. Its four common NOSQL data models are {{c1::key-value, document (JSON), graph and column-based}}.
